Product failed but that might be user error not a faulty product. This review is for "Herbs Botanica Alum Powder Alumbre Potassium Alum Fitkari Fatkari For Skin." The weather? I have no idea. That's the trouble with reviewing a product like this - if it doesn't work, is it the product's fault or is it user error - did I measure something wrong, does it just not work well when it's cold out? I have no idea. So I decided to give it 3 stars - average. Because it does appear to be alum powder, but it being inside a plastic bag instead of another plastic bag seemed stupid and wasteful, and it didn't work for my purposes but as I said I don't know if that was my fault or the product's fault. The cute isn't a cover up... A good number of times when you see something as cute as this little bee-esque slicker brush, the manufacturer is covering up a shoddy product and hoping the "awwww, it's SO CUUUUUUTE!!!!!" factor will overwhelm the buyer so much they don't notice and/or care when the product gives up the ghost after only a few uses. So yes, choosing this slicker based on looks probably wasn't the smartest of choices, but in the end it seems to be a good one. This slicker brush is rather nice (and should be for the $20 price tag). It's comfortable to hold. There is weight to it so this doesn't feel flimsy to where the grooming head will break off if you try to comb out a snarl in your pet's fur, or like the body is the thinnest molded plastic they could get away with so it didn't break just removing it from the packaging. Another plus is the end of the tines are tipped/dipped in protective little drops of plastic so the sharp metal ends don't harm your pet. I've always avoided those slickers as they seem like some kind of torture device - how can bare metal ends be comfortable when raked over skin? For taking care of loose hair, this did a bang up job on our two Maine Coons, including the one who absolutely loathes - and I mean to the depths of H.E. double hockey sticks with a side of utter disgust - being brushed. She was adopted from the shelter as an abused kitty from the home of an older cat hoarder, and whatever happened during her first six years of life there were traumatic enough that she will do her best to eviscerate anyone who tries to groom her long fur beyond the area of her neck. She actually lets us very gently use this on the rest of her back and legs and tail for around 45-60 seconds before flipping out, and that's a big improvement! Who knows, maybe she's as amused by the itty bitty bee antenna as we are, but this is the first slicker brush (even with the safety tipped teeth) she's let us use on her back, sides, and legs. The other Maine Coon (a big chonker of a guy) lays on his back with his legs stretched out and purrs like a race car when he gets groomed, so it's not a surprise that he loves this slicker as well. Cleaning the hair out is easy. Just press the button, the plastic disk pushes up, and the hair is forced off of the tines for easy removal. A few of the finer hairs may stick to the plastic or around the tines, but nothing major. When the slicker gets dirty between the base and the underside of the plastic disk, one of those super skinny reusable straw scrubby brushes and a bit of dish soap does the trick. We clip a wooden clothespin on either side of the plastic disk to keep it raised so the tines can air dry and not rust from trapped moisture. Since the tines all seem to be securely anchored to the base of the slicker head, we aren't too concerned about one being pulled out while trying to work through a tangle. It's still a good idea to check the tines every so often to make sure they are all there, none are loose, and that none of the little safety tips at the end of the tines have come off. The only thing that could improve this slicker is a price reduction. A pair of googly eyes wouldn't hurt, either.

Time to put the razor away! I [RECOMMEND] this roll on wax kit. First time user who is happily throwing away her razor! Pros: ~Reasonably priced ~Easy to find refills ~Easy to use (once you get the swing of it) Cons: ~On/off button and temp buttons in the way while using ~Corded - limits mobility If you still want some more information about this product, please read on! ______________________________________________________________ I was a little apprehensive to use an at-home wax kit. Other than my eyebrows, I have no familiarity with waxing, either in a salon or at home. I was slightly disappointed that the instructions were not clearer for a beginner. My biggest issue is when loading the honey wax - does the lid stay on? Does the tape stay on? I'm still not sure. I loaded it with the lid and tape on and it heated up just fine. The wax cartridge is reusable (unless you use all the wax in one sitting) so I assume you take the lid and tape off, as it is off when you go to reheat and reuse. There is a temperature range that goes up to 125 degrees (f). I was not sure where the temp should be or where my personal heat threshold would be. I set it to 100 degrees (f) and it seemed to do the job. I will probably go hotter the next time around. The wax rolls on nice and easy, the waxing strip is easy to get on and get off. It also comes with 10 finishing wipes, but they did not seem to do anything for me. A couple small issues came up while I was doing this. First, the machine is corded. Not the end of the world, but it does limit where you can do this. Second, the operation buttons are in the middle of the machine. Several times I turned the machine off or lowered the temperature while rolling on my leg. It could be a me thing, and didn't really interrupt the process, just a small issue to note. I tested the wax on my wrist (like you would a baby bottle), and didn't know how to get the wax off after. The finishing wipe didn't work, soap and water didn't work. I used some isopropyl alcohol and a cotton ball to finally get it off. I suppose you could use a wax strip to get it off too, but didn't think off that at the time. Overall, this was a good experience and a great alternative to shaving.

money-saving, time-consuming results. also loud buzz. Contents: 1. Review 2. Mechanism 3. Tips 1. Review I want to provide enough information to anyone who's on the fence due to mixed reviews. I bought this because appointments to electrolysis clinics were back up for months or even years in my area, and were looking to be costly too. Having used this machine for about 4 months, I can say that the results are real and permanent, though very time-consuming. It can be a little uncomfortable depending on your sensitivity and the area you're working on. I've been regularly using it about every week, taking a few hours (4-6?) each session, mainly focusing on my upper lip and chin area. These areas have not been too difficult for me to deal pain-wise with at 6-7 (5 right under the nose) around my lips and full 10 around my chin. For the reference of time taken/amount of hair, I have sparse male facial hair that grows in waves. The last time I used it I was able to count how many visible hairs I wanted to remove, which was about 13. That was not long, but I still spent a couple hours removing some less visible hairs and vellus. The probe is not difficult to insert into my hair follicles, even the thinner vellus hairs, and it is not difficult to re-straighten the probe if you accidentally bend it. However, when straightening with tweezers be careful not to pull out the probe, like I had done. The probe without electricity is not uncomfortable when inside the hair follicle in my opinion, but once electricity flows it can be, especially closer to the nose. One thing to note which might not be apparent is that your skin must be hydrated for the electrolysis to work properly. To let you know when the electricity is flowing, the machine lets off a very loud and annoying beep that lasts for about eight seconds. This is really my only real gripe with the machine. Besides that, each hair will take 2-3 of these cycles before you can remove the hair, hopefully with the sheath, otherwise it is still damaged (which is wanted) and will take less effort with the next treatment once the hair regrows. You could try for more cycles per treatment but you risk further damage to your skin. I have seen damage to my own skin (blood serum leakage and hyperpigmentation) just from regular use but it has healed quite nicely with time. The included tweezers are normally very difficult to use, but for the purpose of removing hairs loosened by the electrolysis process, they do the bare minimum. Nevertheless, I do not recomment using them. As for battery life, I cannot really comment since I have been using rechargeable 9-volt batteries and charging between treatments. 2. Mechanism The machine operates using galvanic electrolysis. The way galvanic electrolysis hair removal works is it uses saltwater and the moisture in your skin (which is kind of like saline in some ways) as an electrolyte in which electricity will flow. Usually, electrolysis is known to be done with two probes suspended in a container of a continuous liquid electrolyte. In this scenario, the probes are separated and the electrolyte is discontinuous. Instead, you have saltwater on your finger surrounding the sleeve as one probe, and the needle-like electrode as the other probe which is suspended in the moisture in your skin surrounding your hair follicle. The electrolysis reaction produces very small amounts of chlorine and hydrogen gas (not enough to cause harm), and lye, which is the base that ultimately kills the follicle. This takes a few seconds, and is why this hair removal method is so time-consuming, and requires adequately-hydrated skin. 3. Tips Use rechargeable 9-volt batteries if you anticipate months of treatment. Also, use numbing cream on sensitive areas like directly under your nose. You can feel the electricity flowing if you have any cuts on your fingers, so be careful. Also, prolonged usage may discolor your fingertips from the metal sleeve. I recommend using a different pair of tweezers that you like to use to remove the treated hairs. I found that air conditioning dehydrated my skin and makes treatment almost impossible. On the other hand, I also found that sweating makes treatment much easier, so I tend to drink hot drinks before and as I treat the hairs. In worst-case scenarios I place a small dab of saltwater on the area of skin around the hair, which usually only works one beep cycle before I need to dab again. I also found that sometimes the metal sleeve is not seated well after I put it back on from cleaning, so I reorient it and test (on my skin) until it works well. I found the comfort testing on a patch of hair before actual treatment to be not very helpful. In my case, I tried the hairs on my fingers which were wildly more sensitive at 5-6 than actually treating my chin, which could handle 10 without much discomfort. YMMV

Very Impressed! When I first bought this product, I was worried by other reviews I saw. Difficulty inserting the probe, the probe breaking shortly after purchase, machine not working, etc. But I'm pleased to say none of these things have happened with mine! The device came with a back up probe, but I've had this device for a month and haven't needed to use it! The probe might bend slightly (I actually prefer mine to have a slight angle to it), but this is quickly resolved by gently bending it back in place. Is it hard to do? Nope! If you're the type of person who regularly plucks hairs in the mirror, using this device is a piece of cake. All it takes is a steady hand, precision, and patience. I treat the hairs I want to remove with a normal, non-magnifying mirror and my phone flashlight. Does it cause scarring? My first time was a bit rough as I was still getting the hang of correct insertion angles. The result of that session was a couple of larger scabs that eventually healed back to normal. When you insert the probe down the hair shaft, sometimes there will be slight swelling directly around the entry point. The day after treatment, you may see small, pinpoint scabs over some entry points. But that is normal and they go away quickly. Is it painful? To me, not at all. Some areas of the body are more sensitive than others. But I use this device mainly on my jawline. Compared to electrolysis appointments I've gone to, the sensation is much less painful! All you feel is a tingling, pinching sensation if the probe is inserted correctly. Overall, purchasing this device instead of spending $200 a month for a 1-hour electrolysis appointment is wayyyy better for my budget and gives the same results.

Works Well, No Instructions. There are no useful instructions on how to use this product. For something like this it typically matters how long it sits or if it is left to dry out. I took a guess and let it sit for one hour. I applied a line of the gel over the threshold of the shower where the door seal sits. This area often accumulates mold. The smell is not as strong as other cleaning solutions I have used, but there is a light chemical smell. It comes with a pair of disposable gloves but I did not use them. Since it is a gel it is fairly easy to handle without making a mess. After one hour I wiped it clean with a damp cloth. On the tile it works about the same as soap and water. It still required some scrubbing in certain areas. On the door seal it performed much better. The areas where the gel was applied cleared up not only the mold, but also the soap scum which would not wipe away with just the wet cloth alone. Overall it seems to work fairly well, but it is hard to say how well with no instructions provided. It may take some trial and error to maximize the performance of the gel.

It totally DOES work, but it is totally A PAIN to use. First of all, a lot of people have said this is useless or that it doesn't work. That isn't remotely true. Versions of this device, in one form or another, have been on the market for like 50 years because they DO work. However, the device has an incredibly steep learning curve, is not intuitive to use, has multiple design problems, and costs way more than it should. One of the frustrating aspects of this device is that all of the probes/needles have a spring base. This is there to prevent an inexperienced user (read basically everyone who buys one of these) from accidentally applying current to a part of their skin other than a follicle and thereby potentially causing skin damage. This is an admirable idea, but in practice it means that unless you are 1,000% on-target with the probe, it will just just constantly bounce around on your skin without going into the follicle, truly a frustrating experience! The probes/needles are also far more expensive than professional electrolysis needles, likely due to the silly spring mechanism. I'll note that there are numerous guides for modifying this device (search Inverness OneTouch modifications if curious) to use pro needles which increases its utility and ease of use but also makes it potentially more dangerous if you don't know what you're doing. Now for the good, this device gives you the ability to perform safe, effective, truly permanent hair removal on yourself and/or your loved ones in the comfort of your own home and at your own pace, accounting for your own comfort level. "Professional" electrologists are all over the place in terms of effectiveness, quality, value, actual, literal professionalism, etc. My experience with them has been uniformly poor despite patronizing nearly a dozen at this point. This is cheaper, more convenient, and, assuming you know what you're doing, more likely to be effective on a permanent basis than professional treatment, especially if the electrologist in question is not a 100% galvanic operator (this device is an unsophisticated example of a 100% galvanic machine). Just wish it were a little bit less frustrating to use!

Works really well, but even getting 2 in 1, it’s pricier than my go-to drugstore liquid liners. This comes in an outer product box. It is made in Korea. The product page says it is cruelty free and vegan, but I didn’t see any kind of certified logo saying it was on the product box. It is free of parabens, sulfates, gluten, and “other harsh chemicals.” This is a dual ended liquid liner. One end has a felt tip and one end has a brush tip. The caps are labeled, which is great! I don’t have to pull off the tops every time to figure out which end is which! Of course, since the labels are on the CAPS, you have to make sure not to mix them up. I don’t see myself having an issue with that since I don’t ever see a reason I’d take off both ends at the same time. But, if you do, you definitely want to make sure to put the correct cap on the correct side so you don’t mix them up. It probably would have been better for them to put the label on the center part rather than the caps, but it’s fine as long as you don’t take both ends off at the same time or just make sure to put the right caps back on. Both ends work really well. They glide on easily without skipping or bleeding. They are a pigmented black, not thin or watery black. They dry down quickly and stay in place throughout the day without smudging or coming off. I have really small, really hooded eyes, so having a dual ended eyeliner pen is great! I have the brush tip to get the thin tightline I want on my upper lash line, then I have the thicker felt tip to do my little wing when I want to. Both work great. When I first saw it was priced at $28.50, I thought that was pretty darn pricey for an eyeliner. But, it is dual ended, so you’re getting 2 eyeliners in 1 pen. Looking at it that way, it’s $14.25 a pen. I usually spend somewhere around $8-10 on my usual ones at the drugstore, so $14.25 isn’t the cheapest, but it isn’t too bad either. Personally, I love it being dual ended, but not enough to spend more than I spend on my usual liquid liners. My usual one at the drugstore ones are $10 (NYX Epic Wear Liquid Liner) and $8 (Maybelline Curvitude Angled Liquid Liner) and I never have any issues with them. So, I don’t see myself spending $28.50, even if I’m getting 2 for 1 because that’s still $14.25 each, which is more than I usually spend on my liquid liners. If price isn’t an issue for you, this is a really good liquid liner. Both ends work great and it’s a nice formula. I give it 4 stars.

Cleansing them from the outside wasn't working, so I tried these "Ear Sticks." The green portion is sturdy enough (but not overly stiff) that I could easily get it into my ear. The rest of it (the white paper) on the other hand ... Dry, they look like they're small enough to fit through a standard piercing hole. However, once you soak them in the provided solution, they end up a little too big to comfortably fit through. I was afraid to just pull them through, thinking that would cause damage, so I gently twisted them through. It still caused damage. Both holes were bleeding when I was done. The solution smells nice, for some reason. (Well, it's because they added fragrance, but I was expecting a plain saline solution, or something similar. Fragrance doesn't seem like a good idea if you're trying to avoid infections, but I'm no doctor.) Bottom line: if you have bigger holes (maybe 12/14 gauge?), this may work for you. If you went to the jeweler's (or Claire's) to get your ears (or wherever) pierced, I would not recommend it.
